01 / Introduction

Introduction and scope

Value at Risk locates a loss threshold. Expected Shortfall describes the severity of the tail beyond that threshold. Understanding both requires a probability model, a valuation rule and a precise definition of the loss being measured.

The Markowitz project summarized portfolio uncertainty through means, variances and covariances. That is a natural language for diversification, but two portfolios with the same volatility can have very different extreme losses. A symmetric bell-shaped distribution, a distribution with occasional jumps and a short-option payoff need not have comparable tails. This guide moves from dispersion around the centre to the upper end of a loss distribution.

A risk number is a statement about a specified experiment. Hold today's portfolio fixed, choose a horizon, describe the changes in market factors over that horizon, revalue the positions and ask how the resulting losses are distributed. Alter the positions, the horizon, the scenario probabilities or the valuation model and the number changes. A forecast of tomorrow's risk and a measurement of the last year's realized losses answer different questions even when they use the same formula.

An analogy: the flood line and the water above it

Imagine recording water levels beside a river. A high quantile identifies a level exceeded on a small fraction of days. It does not tell you how high the river rises on those days. VaR is the flood line; ES is the average water level in the specified upper tail. The analogy explains the distinction, while the mathematics handles probability masses and finite samples more carefully than an ordinary average of “flood days”.

Reading path

Part I establishes loss conventions, quantiles, the definition of ES, coherence and analytical distributions. Part II develops historical, weighted, parametric, Monte Carlo and extreme-value estimation, then connects risk to dependence, attribution and optimization. Part III treats validation, uncertainty and numerical practice. The laboratory compares analytical risk with empirical estimates from a reproducible synthetic sample.

All figures on this page are computed from the stated synthetic assumptions. They illustrate mechanisms rather than report empirical findings about a particular market. Hover over a plotted line to inspect the underlying coordinates; a shared cross-section shows the values of other visible curves at the same horizontal position. The calculations and graphics remain inside this HTML file, and the static notes work without a network connection.

Prerequisites and boundaries

Basic probability, expectations, standard deviation, conditional distributions and differentiation are sufficient for the main chapters. Matrix notation appears in portfolio aggregation and risk contributions; likelihood ratios appear in backtesting. The Monte Carlo notes explain sampling and simulation error in more detail. The Black–Scholes notes provide the valuation model used in the option example.

The focus is market-risk loss distributions. Credit migration, default, operational events, funding constraints and liquidation costs can also enter a loss model, but require additional structure. VaR and ES compress information into one number each. They should be read alongside scenarios, exposures and an account of model uncertainty, rather than as complete descriptions of every possible loss.

02 / Definitions

Profit, loss and the risk horizon

Use a positive number for a loss and a negative number for a gain. Let VtV_t be current portfolio value and let Vt+hV_{t+h} be the value at horizon hh, with cash flows handled consistently. A simple frozen-position convention is:

Πt,h=Vt+h−Vt,Lt,h=−Πt,h=Vt−Vt+h.\Pi_{t,h}=V_{t+h}-V_t,\qquad L_{t,h}=-\Pi_{t,h}=V_t-V_{t+h}.
(01)

If dividends, coupons, option exercise payments or funding costs occur inside the horizon, define whether they are included in total wealth or added separately to profit and loss. A bond price drop on a coupon date is not automatically an economic loss: the coupon may offset it. For a self-financing portfolio, the comparison must include the cash account. Document the convention before estimating the distribution.

For wealth W>0W>0 invested in assets with simple returns RiR_i, fixed initial capital weights wiw_i and no additional cash-flow complication, the return-based approximation is:

Rp=∑i=1dwiRi,L=−WRp.R_p=\sum_{i=1}^{d}w_iR_i,\qquad L=-W R_p.
(02)

The minus sign reverses the tail: bad portfolio returns become large positive losses. A 2% loss on €1,000,000 is €20,000. A reported “99% return VaR” may refer to the negative 1% return quantile, while a “99% loss VaR” is the positive 99% loss quantile. These conventions describe the same adverse region in a continuous distribution, but the displayed signs differ.

Horizon, confidence and units

The horizon determines how long positions are exposed. The confidence level determines how far into the loss distribution the measurement looks. A one-day 99% VaR and a ten-day 97.5% ES are different functionals of potentially different distributions; they cannot be compared by reading their currency values alone. State currency, horizon, confidence, position convention and model date together.

Currency risk scales with wealth when losses are proportional to exposure. Percentage risk divides the currency result by the same positive wealth base. Log returns are additive over time, while simple returns compound; a log-return threshold cannot be substituted directly into a simple-return P&L equation. For a single long asset with log return rr, exact loss is W(1−er)W(1-e^r), which differs from −Wr-Wr in large moves.

Physical scenarios and pricing probabilities

Risk forecasting generally describes market moves under a real-world, or physical, probability model ℙ\mathbb P. A derivative may then be revalued in each scenario using a risk-neutral pricing model ℚ\mathbb Q. The scenario probability and the option valuation rule have different jobs. A discounted risk-neutral expected payoff is an option price; it is not automatically a forecast of the distribution of tomorrow's trading losses.

A frozen-position horizon measures changes in today's book. Actual future P&L also reflects new trades, hedging, fees and position changes. Both are useful, but a backtest must identify which P&L is being compared with which forecast. A forecast made before trading tomorrow should never use tomorrow's closing volatility estimate as an input.

03 / Probability

Distribution functions and quantiles

The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, of loss LL gives the probability that the loss does not exceed a specified value. It is nondecreasing and right-continuous, including when losses occur at a finite set of values.

FL(ℓ)=ℙ(L≤ℓ),qα(L)=inf{ℓ:FL(ℓ)≥α},0<α<1.F_L(\ell)=\mathbb P(L\le\ell),\qquad q_\alpha(L)=\inf\{\ell:F_L(\ell)\ge\alpha\},\quad 0<\alpha<1.
(03)

The quantile is the first loss level whose accumulated probability reaches the target confidence. With a continuous, strictly increasing CDF, this is the familiar inverse FL−1(α)F_L^{-1}(\alpha). With a discrete distribution, the CDF has jumps and the quantile lies at an atom. The inverse-CDF definition still works; a numerical interpolation between adjacent observations defines a different sample convention.

Write FL(qα−)F_L(q_\alpha-) for the probability strictly below the quantile. The defining inequalities are:

FL(qα−)≤α≤FL(qα),ℙ(L>qα)≤1−α.F_L(q_\alpha-)\le\alpha\le F_L(q_\alpha),\qquad \mathbb P(L>q_\alpha)\le1-\alpha.
(04)

For a continuous distribution with no mass at the quantile, equality holds in the exceedance probability. With an atom, strictly greater losses can occupy less than the specified upper-tail probability. This distinction is central to both ES estimation and exception counting. Counting losses equal to VaR as breaches changes the probability statement.

The quantile transformation

If UU is uniform on (0,1)(0,1), the random variable qU(L)q_U(L) has the same distribution as LL. Imagine the probability axis as a line of equally likely tickets. The quantile function assigns a loss to each ticket in increasing order. A flat section of the quantile curve assigns many tickets to the same loss; this is an atom in the loss distribution.

This representation turns an average over part of the loss distribution into an integral over probability. The upper tail is simply the interval from α\alpha to one. It also explains why an empirical distribution gives equal probability to observations before ties are aggregated, and why an ES estimator must sometimes use a fraction of one observation's probability mass.

Numerical conventions

For NN observations ordered as L(1)≤⋯≤L(N)L_{(1)}\le\cdots\le L_{(N)}, the inverse empirical CDF uses index ⌈Nα⌉\lceil N\alpha\rceil, with indices starting at one. Some software uses linear interpolation or another quantile rule by default. Neither choice should be hidden: a finite-sample discrepancy can be entirely due to conventions rather than a coding error. This page uses the inverse empirical CDF throughout.

Quantiles need not vary smoothly. An empirical VaR can remain unchanged as confidence rises, then jump to the next observation. Differentiating such a curve as if it were a smooth population quantile is misleading. Smooth asymptotic results later in the guide require a positive, regular density near the target quantile.

04 / Risk measures

Value at Risk: definition and interpretation

At confidence α\alpha, Value at Risk is the α\alpha-quantile of the loss distribution:

VaRα(L)=qα(L).\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L)=q_\alpha(L).
(05)

For a continuous model, a one-day 99% VaR of €23,263 says that the model assigns a 1% probability to a one-day loss greater than €23,263. It does not say that €23,263 is the maximum possible loss. It also does not promise that precisely one day out of every hundred realized days will exceed the threshold. Even a correctly calibrated model produces random counts and runs of exceptions.

A quantile is a location, not a severity average

VaR records where the upper tail begins. Moving losses that are already far above that boundary even further upward can leave VaR unchanged. The distribution may become much more dangerous while retaining the same threshold. This is why a VaR limit alone can fail to distinguish a moderately bad tail from one containing a small probability of catastrophic losses.

Confidence is a model probability, not confidence in the model's accuracy. A 99% VaR computed from a badly specified distribution does not become reliable merely because the confidence level is high. A statistical confidence interval for an estimated VaR is a different object: it describes uncertainty in the quantile estimate across samples.

Signs, limits and aggregation

VaR may be negative. If a position has a sufficiently certain gain over the horizon, its upper loss quantile can still lie below zero. Clipping the result to zero changes the risk measure. An operational limit system may apply such a floor, but should label it as a reporting rule rather than the mathematical VaR.

A portfolio VaR should be calculated from the distribution of the combined loss, with dependence respected. Adding standalone VaRs is not a general aggregation rule. The combined quantile depends on which individual losses occur together, and VaR does not always satisfy the diversification inequality introduced in Chapter 6.

VaR remains useful as an interpretable threshold, a forecasting target and a reference for exception counts. Its limitations concern what is omitted and how aggregation behaves, rather than making every quantile estimate uninformative. The natural companion is a measure that describes the entire selected upper tail.

05 / Risk measures

Expected Shortfall and probability mass

Expected Shortfall averages the worst 1−α1-\alpha fraction of the loss distribution, counting probability mass rather than just counting observations strictly above a threshold. For integrable losses its general definition is:

ESα(L)=11−α∫α1qu(L)du.\operatorname{ES}_\alpha(L)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\int_\alpha^1 q_u(L)\,du.
(06)

The quantile-ticket analogy gives a direct interpretation: average the losses attached to the last 1−α1-\alpha fraction of tickets. ES is expressed in the same units as the loss. Since the quantile curve is nondecreasing, ES is at least VaR at the same confidence level. It can be equal when the entire selected tail has the same loss.

Continuous and discrete distributions

For a continuous distribution with a unique quantile and no atom at that point, ES equals the conditional mean of losses exceeding VaR. With discrete distributions, averaging all losses greater than or equal to VaR can include too much probability mass; averaging strictly greater losses can include too little. The general identity is:

ESα(L)=𝔼[L𝟙{L>qα}]+qα(FL(qα)−α)1−α.\operatorname{ES}_\alpha(L)=\frac{\mathbb E[L\mathbb 1_{\{L>q_\alpha\}}]+q_\alpha(F_L(q_\alpha)-\alpha)}{1-\alpha}.
(07)

The first term includes all losses strictly above the quantile. The second adds only the portion of the boundary atom needed to complete the specified tail mass. An equivalent formula, convenient for computation, is:

ESα(L)=qα+𝔼[(L−qα)+]1−α,x+=max(x,0).\operatorname{ES}_\alpha(L)=q_\alpha+\frac{\mathbb E[(L-q_\alpha)_+]}{1-\alpha}, \qquad x_+=\max(x,0).
(08)

Consider losses of 0, 10 and 100 with probabilities 94%, 4% and 2%. At 95% confidence the quantile is 10. The worst 5% consists of all the 2% mass at 100 and 3% of the mass at 10, giving ES =(0.02×100+0.03×10)/0.05=46=(0.02\times100+0.03\times10)/0.05=46. The conditional mean given loss at least 10 is 40; the conditional mean given loss greater than 10 is 100. Neither equals the required fractional-tail average.

The distinction matters for rounded observations, credit losses, payoff atoms and every empirical distribution. The coherent definition follows the probability-mass treatment discussed by Acerbi and Tasche (2002). Terms such as CVaR, tail mean and conditional tail expectation are used with differing conventions in the literature; verify the actual definition when comparing results.

Existence and interpretation

A finite VaR can exist when ES is infinite. A tail distribution with sufficiently slow probability decay can have finite quantiles at every confidence below one and still have an infinite tail mean. Estimating a finite ES from a finite sample does not establish that the population ES exists: a sample has a largest observation, while the model may have no upper bound.

ES is an average conditional on being in a selected probability tail, not the expected loss over all outcomes. It is also not a maximum. Losses beyond ES remain possible. Read it as a severity summary with explicit confidence and horizon, and inspect the tail model responsible for that summary.

06 / Mathematical properties

Coherence and diversification

A monetary risk measure maps a random loss to a capital-like quantity. Under the positive-loss convention, adding a certain loss increases risk by that amount. Four properties define coherence on a suitable linear space of integrable losses:

L1≤L2⇒ρ(L1)≤ρ(L2),ρ(L+c)=ρ(L)+c.L_1\le L_2\Rightarrow\rho(L_1)\le\rho(L_2),\qquad \rho(L+c)=\rho(L)+c.
(09)
ρ(aL)=aρ(L)(a≥0),ρ(L1+L2)≤ρ(L1)+ρ(L2).\rho(aL)=a\rho(L)\quad(a\ge0),\qquad \rho(L_1+L_2)\le\rho(L_1)+\rho(L_2).
(10)

These are monotonicity, translation equivariance, positive homogeneity and subadditivity. Monotonicity compares outcomes scenario by scenario. Translation describes a sure cash loss. Homogeneity expresses proportional exposure scaling. Subadditivity says that combined risk should not exceed the sum of standalone risks. It is a statement about diversification and aggregation, not a promise that every combination reduces risk strictly.

ES satisfies these properties when defined through the quantile integral with the required integrability. VaR satisfies the first three but can fail subadditivity. Under special distributional assumptions, such as jointly normal losses at confidence above 50%, VaR behaves subadditively through the standard-deviation aggregation rule. That special case should not be generalized to arbitrary losses.

A concrete VaR counterexample

Let each of two independent exposures lose 100 with probability 4%, otherwise zero. At 95% confidence, each standalone VaR is zero. The combined loss is zero with probability 0.962=0.92160.96^2=0.9216, 100 with probability 0.0768 and 200 with probability 0.0016. Its 95% quantile is 100. Thus combining the positions increases VaR from a standalone sum of zero to 100.

Individual ES is 80 because the worst 5% includes 4% probability at loss 100 and 1% at zero. Combined ES is 103.2, using all 0.16% probability at 200 and 4.84% at 100. It is below the sum of individual ES values, 160. The example demonstrates a property of the functional, rather than an assertion that the combined exposure is harmless.

Convexity and diversification incentives

Positive homogeneity and subadditivity imply convexity:

ρ(λL1+(1−λ)L2)≤λρ(L1)+(1−λ)ρ(L2),0≤λ≤1.\rho(\lambda L_1+(1-\lambda)L_2)\le \lambda\rho(L_1)+(1-\lambda)\rho(L_2),\qquad 0\le\lambda\le1.
(11)

For portfolio optimization, convexity creates a tractable landscape when loss is affine in positions and the feasible set is convex. It does not guarantee stable estimated weights: an optimization can be mathematically convex while depending strongly on a few extreme scenarios. Nor does it incorporate transaction costs or nonlinear liquidation impact unless those features enter the loss map.

The cash sign convention differs in papers that model future wealth rather than losses. In a future-wealth convention, adding cash reduces required capital. Here the same economic property is written for losses, so adding a certain loss increases the risk value. Translate conventions before comparing formulas.

07 / Analytical models

Normal loss distributions

Suppose loss is a location-scale transformation of a standard normal variable, with mean mm and standard deviation s>0s>0. Let Φ\Phi and φ\phi denote the standard normal CDF and density, and let zα=Φ−1(α)z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(\alpha).

L=m+sZ,Z∼N(0,1),VaRα=m+szα.L=m+sZ,\quad Z\sim N(0,1),\qquad \operatorname{VaR}_\alpha=m+s z_\alpha.
(12)

Substitute into the continuous-tail conditional expectation. Since φ'(z)=−zφ(z)\phi'(z)=-z\phi(z), integrating zφ(z)z\phi(z) from the quantile to infinity gives φ(zα)\phi(z_\alpha). Therefore:

ESα=m+sφ(zα)1−α.\operatorname{ES}_\alpha=m+s\frac{\phi(z_\alpha)}{1-\alpha}.
(13)

At 99% confidence, the normal VaR multiplier is approximately 2.32635 and the ES multiplier approximately 2.66521. At 97.5%, the multipliers are approximately 1.95996 and 2.33780. Their difference measures the mean distance from the quantile into the specified normal tail. They are distribution-specific constants, not universal conversion factors.

Return-to-loss conversion

If a portfolio's simple return is normal with mean μp\mu_p and standard deviation σp\sigma_p, then m=−Wμpm=-W\mu_p and s=Wσps=W\sigma_p. A positive expected return reduces expected loss and shifts both risk measures downward. This conversion is exact for a linear simple-return loss map, although the assumed normal distribution permits returns below −100% and can be unsuitable for extreme-horizon asset modeling.

For a €1,000,000 portfolio with zero expected one-day return and 1% daily volatility, normal 99% VaR is €23,263.48 and ES is €26,652.14. The mean is set to zero to isolate tail mechanics. If expected daily return is 0.05%, both figures decrease by €500 under the same model, because this adds a deterministic shift to loss.

Estimation and model assumptions

The formulas require only two parameters, but that apparent simplicity transfers responsibility to the normality assumption. A fitted standard deviation averages squared deviations across the sample. It does not independently identify the shape of an extreme tail. Normal VaR can be precisely computed and still be a poor risk forecast if losses have skewness, jumps or heavy tails.

Parameter uncertainty is separate from evaluating the analytical formula. A known-parameter normal model has exact risk values; replacing its mean and volatility with estimates creates uncertainty. Conditional volatility models introduce another layer: the formula may be normal conditional on today's information even when the unconditional mixture is heavy-tailed.

When s=0s=0, loss is deterministic. Both VaR and ES equal mm, including if mm is negative. Code should handle this directly rather than dividing by zero in a density or quantile calculation. An estimated covariance matrix that produces a slightly negative variance through numerical error needs diagnosis, not a silent reinterpretation as a random negative volatility.

08 / Analytical models

Student-t distributions and heavy tails

A Student-t variable has a tail that decays polynomially rather than with the normal distribution's exponential quadratic decay. Degrees of freedom ν\nu control the tail thickness. Small ν\nu assigns more probability to extreme observations, while large ν\nu approaches the normal model.

L=m+aTν,VaRα=m+atν,α,tν,α=Fν−1(α).L=m+aT_\nu,\qquad \operatorname{VaR}_\alpha=m+a\,t_{\nu,\alpha}, \quad t_{\nu,\alpha}=F_\nu^{-1}(\alpha).
(14)

The scale aa is not generally the standard deviation. For ν>2\nu>2, the variance of a standard Student-t variable is ν/(ν−2)\nu/(\nu-2). To compare models with the same finite standard deviation ss, use:

a=sν−2ν,ν>2.a=s\sqrt{\frac{\nu-2}{\nu}},\qquad \nu>2.
(15)

Let fνf_\nu be the standard Student-t density. Integrating its upper first moment yields the ES formula:

ESα=m+aν+tν,α2ν−1fν(tν,α)1−α,ν>1.\operatorname{ES}_\alpha =m+a\frac{\nu+t_{\nu,\alpha}^{\,2}}{\nu-1} \frac{f_\nu(t_{\nu,\alpha})}{1-\alpha},\qquad \nu>1.
(16)

The ES formula requires a finite first moment, so ν>1\nu>1. The matched-volatility expression for aa requires ν>2\nu>2. A Student-t model with 1<ν≤21<\nu\le2 can have finite ES but infinite variance; it can be parameterized by scale, but cannot be assigned a finite population standard deviation. For ν≤1\nu\le1, the upper-tail mean diverges even though every quantile below one is finite.

What a matched-volatility comparison shows

Equal variance does not imply equal VaR at every confidence. The rescaled Student-t distribution concentrates more mass near the centre while retaining much heavier extreme tails. At some moderate quantiles its VaR can be below the normal VaR; sufficiently deep in the tail it overtakes it. ES is especially sensitive because it averages the distribution beyond the boundary.

For ν=5\nu=5, the matched standard-deviation scale is 3/5\sqrt{3/5}. Chapter 27 compares this model with the normal distribution across several confidence levels using identical wealth and volatility. Changing ν\nu while accidentally holding aa, rather than ss, fixed mixes a variance change with a tail-shape change. The laboratory avoids that confusion by accepting standard deviation as an input.

Fitting and simulation

A Student-t variable can be simulated as Z/U/νZ/\sqrt{U/\nu}, where ZZ is standard normal, UU is chi-squared with ν\nu degrees of freedom, and the variables are independent. The denominator occasionally becomes small, creating extreme observations. This is a useful analogy for a market whose apparent noise scale itself changes from one scenario to another.

Estimated degrees of freedom can be unstable in a short sample because the most informative observations are rare. Maximum likelihood under a t model is a parametric assumption, not evidence that every future crisis follows that same distribution. Check tail diagnostics, parameter sensitivity and out-of-sample calibration before treating a fitted tail multiplier as a fixed constant.

09 / Portfolios

Portfolio aggregation and dependence

Let the vector of simple asset returns have mean μ\mu and covariance matrix Σ\Sigma. A portfolio with fixed weights ww and positive wealth WW has the following mean loss and loss standard deviation under a linear return map:

mp=−WwTμ,sp=WwTΣw.m_p=-Ww^{\mathsf T}\mu,\qquad s_p=W\sqrt{w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w}.
(17)

If the returns are jointly normal, portfolio loss is normal and the analytical formulas apply. Covariance is enough in this setting because a multivariate normal distribution is determined by its means and covariance. For non-normal joint distributions, matching the same covariance matrix does not determine the portfolio tail.

For two equal-volatility, zero-mean losses with correlation ρ\rho, equal weights give:

sp=s1+ρ2.s_p=s\sqrt{\frac{1+\rho}{2}}.
(18)

At correlation one there is no volatility diversification. At zero correlation the portfolio standard deviation is s/2s/\sqrt2. At correlation minus one, equal opposing fluctuations cancel in this idealized model. A covariance matrix must be positive semidefinite; selecting arbitrary pairwise correlations in a larger system can violate that requirement and create impossible combinations.

Dependence belongs to scenarios

Historical simulation preserves observed same-date factor combinations if entire scenario rows are used. Independently shuffling each asset's returns destroys that dependence. A Monte Carlo model must likewise simulate jointly: a matrix factor such as Cholesky can transform independent normal shocks into correlated normal shocks, but a non-Gaussian dependence model requires more than the same linear transformation.

The portfolio loss distribution depends on both marginal behavior and the joint arrangement of outcomes. An analogy is a group of fire alarms: knowing each alarm's probability of sounding tells you little about how many will sound simultaneously if a common cause can trigger them. Tail dependence measures one aspect of such simultaneous extremes and is treated separately in Chapter 18.

Positions and revaluation

Returns aggregate through initial capital weights for simple, fixed holdings. Derivative books are often expressed through quantities, contract multipliers and nonlinear pricing functions rather than return weights. An option with near-zero initial value can have enormous percentage returns, so normalizing its risk by its own premium can be misleading. Aggregate currency P&L first and use a clearly defined portfolio capital base if reporting percentages.

Correlation stress is useful, but scenario consistency matters. A stressed dependence matrix must still define a valid joint model. Replacing all correlations with a high positive value can harm some long-only portfolios while benefiting positions with opposite signs. Inspect the actual loss map rather than assuming that “higher correlation” always increases every book's risk.

10 / Time aggregation

Horizon scaling and temporal dependence

For independent, identically distributed additive daily normal losses with mean mm, standard deviation ss and unchanged exposures, the hh-day sum is normal. Its risk measures are:

VaRα,h=hm+hszα,ESα,h=hm+hsφ(zα)1−α.\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha,h}=hm+\sqrt h\,s z_\alpha,\qquad \operatorname{ES}_{\alpha,h}=hm+\sqrt h\,s\frac{\phi(z_\alpha)}{1-\alpha}.
(19)

The mean grows linearly with time, while standard deviation grows with the square root of time. Multiplying the entire one-day VaR by h\sqrt h is exact here only when the mean term is zero, or happens to vanish. The general expression must separate location and dispersion.

Where the square-root rule breaks

For stationary daily losses with autocovariance γk\gamma_k, the variance of the sum is:

Var(∑j=1hLj)=hγ0+2∑k=1h−1(h−k)γk.\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{h}L_j\right) =h\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{h-1}(h-k)\gamma_k.
(20)

Positive autocovariance raises variance above the independence rule; negative autocovariance can reduce it. Uncorrelated returns are not necessarily independent. Volatility clustering can make multi-day conditional risk depart from square-root scaling even when raw return autocorrelation is small. Heavy-tailed daily losses also need not retain the same distributional shape after aggregation.

Compounded returns, changing exposures, option gamma, time decay, exercise and margin calls introduce further differences. A multi-day option P&L is not a sum of identically distributed one-day fixed-Greek losses. If rebalancing is part of the strategy, the simulated loss should follow the specified trading rule through the horizon.

Choose a horizon calculation deliberately

One approach uses directly observed multi-day scenarios, with sufficient history and an explicit overlap convention. Another simulates daily market dynamics and revalues the position at the final horizon or through a trading policy. A third uses an analytical aggregation model whose assumptions are appropriate. The square-root rule is a shortcut within a model, rather than a universal identity.

Overlapping hh-day losses share daily observations. This increases the nominal number of windows while inducing dependence, so an IID standard error or exception test is no longer automatically valid. A 250-day history cannot be turned into hundreds of independent ten-day losses simply by shifting a rolling window one day at a time.

Regulatory liquidity-horizon adjustments have their own prescribed construction. They should not be inferred from this simple IID benchmark. The regulatory overview in Chapter 21 identifies the official framework separately from the mathematical scaling example.

11 / Estimation methods

Historical simulation and empirical tails

Historical simulation applies recorded market-factor changes to today's positions, revalues the portfolio and gives the resulting loss scenarios empirical probabilities. For a fixed linear portfolio, applying past return vectors to today's weights may be sufficient. For a derivative book, historical factor shocks generally need to be passed through today's valuation models.

Using past realized portfolio P&L instead answers a different question if positions changed. Today's short option and last year's long stock are different exposures. A historical scenario engine should preserve same-date factor moves, transform them consistently and calculate what today's book would lose under those moves.

Exact empirical VaR and ES

For equally weighted losses, order the observations and use the inverse empirical CDF:

q^α=L(⌈Nα⌉),ES^α=q^α+1N(1−α)∑i=1N(Li−q^α)+.\widehat q_\alpha=L_{(\lceil N\alpha\rceil)},\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{ES}}_\alpha =\widehat q_\alpha+\frac{1}{N(1-\alpha)} \sum_{i=1}^{N}(L_i-\widehat q_\alpha)_+.
(21)

Let b=N(1−α)b=N(1-\alpha), k=⌊b⌋k=\lfloor b\rfloor and r=b−kr=b-k. ES can equivalently be calculated by summing the kk largest observations, adding fraction rr of the next-largest observation and dividing by bb. When r=0r=0, no fractional observation is needed. When b<1b<1, empirical ES equals the largest observed loss.

For ten losses 0,1,…,90,1,\ldots,9 at 85% confidence, VaR is 8. Tail mass in observation units is 1.5, so ES =(9+0.5×8)/1.5=8.66667=(9+0.5\times8)/1.5=8.66667. An average of only losses strictly above VaR gives 9 and omits the required boundary mass. This is a finite-sample definition issue, not a subtle asymptotic adjustment.

What the method assumes

An empirical distribution assumes that its observations, possibly after filtering, are representative of the forecast distribution. A long window offers more tail observations but can mix old regimes with current conditions. A short window adapts faster but leaves fewer rare outcomes. At 99% confidence, 250 observations supply only 2.5 observations' worth of tail mass, regardless of how smooth the histogram looks.

Historical simulation does not impose a normal density, but it is still a model. It selects a window, a weighting rule, shock transformations and a repricing convention. Plain empirical risk cannot infer losses beyond the largest observed scenario. A missing crisis is not assigned positive probability merely because the method is described as nonparametric.

Practical data choices

Align calendars and timestamps across markets. Treat stock splits, coupon dates and missing prices deliberately. A stale price may look like a zero return followed by an oversized move when trading resumes. Pooling unaligned returns can distort dependence and tail attribution. Using total-return data is appropriate for a return-based wealth model, while derivatives may require separate spot, rate, volatility and dividend shocks.

Record how scenarios are mapped to current levels. Absolute rate changes and relative equity moves behave differently, and a historical negative rate move must not create an invalid input through an arbitrary transformation. Historical simulation gains credibility from a well-defined scenario pipeline, rather than from avoiding a named parametric distribution.

12 / Estimation methods

Weighted historical simulation

Assign each historical scenario probability pi≥0p_i\ge0, with probabilities summing to one. The weighted empirical CDF accumulates probabilities rather than observation counts:

F^(ℓ)=∑i=1Npi𝟙{Li≤ℓ},ES^α=q^α+∑ipi(Li−q^α)+1−α.\widehat F(\ell)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_i\mathbb 1_{\{L_i\le\ell\}},\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{ES}}_\alpha =\widehat q_\alpha+\frac{\sum_i p_i(L_i-\widehat q_\alpha)_+}{1-\alpha}.
(22)

Sort losses while keeping each observation attached to its own probability. The weighted quantile is the first loss whose cumulative weight reaches α\alpha. The tail then takes full probability from larger losses and the required fraction of probability at the quantile. Averaging the largest fixed number of observations is wrong once probabilities differ.

Exponential recency weights

A common rule gives observation age j=0j=0 to the newest scenario and uses a decay factor 0<λ<10<\lambda<1:

pj=(1−λ)λj1−λN,Neff=1∑j=0N−1pj2.p_j=\frac{(1-\lambda)\lambda^j}{1-\lambda^N},\qquad N_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}p_j^2}.
(23)

The normalization is important for a finite window. The effective sample size equals NN under equal weights and falls as probability becomes concentrated in a small set of observations. It is a useful measure of weighting concentration, not a universal replacement for the sample size in all confidence intervals. Temporal dependence further reduces information.

Recency weighting resembles listening more closely to the latest weather reports while still remembering older days. It responds to recent conditions, but an old extreme event can gradually lose almost all of its weight. Whether that is sensible depends on the intended forecast. A separate stress scenario may preserve information about events that a rapidly decaying estimation window would largely forget.

Weighted estimation is not volatility filtering

Weighting changes scenario probabilities. Filtering rescales shocks according to estimated market conditions. The methods can be combined, but their effects differ. An old 3% move may receive low recency probability under weighting; under filtering it may instead be standardized by old volatility and rescaled to a current volatility forecast.

Observe the largest individual scenario weight. If one scenario has more probability than the selected tail, ES can consist entirely of that scenario's loss. A large nominal database does not guarantee a well-supported 99.9% tail when a few recent dates dominate its probability distribution.

For weighted portfolios, attach probabilities to whole scenario rows. Using different date weights for different assets and then combining their marginal quantiles generally does not define the same joint empirical distribution. The scenario model must remain internally consistent.

13 / Estimation methods

Parametric and delta-normal models

A parametric model specifies a distribution family and estimates its parameters. The delta-normal method adds a first-order approximation to portfolio revaluation. Let XX be a vector of market factors, dd a vector of position sensitivities and cc a deterministic approximation to carry and passage of time.

ΔV≈c+dTΔX,L≈−c−dTΔX.\Delta V\approx c+d^{\mathsf T}\Delta X,\qquad L\approx-c-d^{\mathsf T}\Delta X.
(24)

If factor changes are multivariate normal with mean μX\mu_X and covariance ΣX\Sigma_X, the approximate loss parameters are:

mL=−c−dTμX,sL2=dTΣXd.m_L=-c-d^{\mathsf T}\mu_X,\qquad s_L^2=d^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_X d.
(25)

Apply the normal VaR and ES formulas to these parameters. Sensitivities must match factor units. Equity delta per unit of spot is not the same object as sensitivity per percentage return. A rate duration expressed per one percentage point must be converted if rate changes are stored as decimals. Unit errors can produce risk values wrong by factors of 100 or 10,000.

Factor mapping

A large book can contain many instruments but relatively few core risk drivers. Mapping bonds to curve nodes, options to spot and volatility factors, and foreign positions to FX exposures can reduce dimensionality. The mapping itself creates approximation error if instruments are represented by inappropriate proxy factors or if relevant basis risk is omitted.

Estimate a covariance matrix on a horizon and calendar consistent with the forecast. A daily covariance combined with weekly sensitivities or mismatched close times can misrepresent exposure. Covariance shrinkage, factor structure and robust estimation can improve conditioning, but should be evaluated in relation to the risk forecast rather than chosen solely for numerical convenience.

Alternative parametric families

A multivariate Student-t model can retain analytical linear-portfolio risk if it is specified as a common-scale elliptical model. If SS is its scale matrix, the covariance is νS/(ν−2)\nu S/(\nu-2) for ν>2\nu>2. A linear combination has scale dTSd\sqrt{d^{\mathsf T}S d}. Confusing the scale matrix with covariance reproduces the univariate scale error from Chapter 8.

Assigning independent univariate t variables to correlated factors is not the same as a multivariate t model with a shared random scale. Dependence assumptions determine aggregate tails. Skewed distributions, mixtures and jump models can be useful, but generally require numerical quantiles and tail integration rather than a single normal multiplier.

Delta-normal risk is fast and transparent, making it useful for explanations and routine diagnostics. Its two main approximations—linear P&L and normal factor moves—should be evaluated separately. Better modeling of one does not automatically repair the other.

14 / Nonlinear positions

Delta–gamma and full revaluation

Options and other nonlinear instruments respond differently to small and large factor moves. A second-order expansion adds curvature to the first-order sensitivity:

ΔV≈c+dTΔX+12ΔXTGΔX,L=−ΔV.\Delta V\approx c+d^{\mathsf T}\Delta X+ \frac12\Delta X^{\mathsf T}G\Delta X,\qquad L=-\Delta V.
(26)

The matrix GG contains second derivatives with respect to the chosen factors. Even with normal factor changes, a quadratic P&L is not generally normal. Applying the normal formula to its fitted mean and variance may miss skewness and tail shape. Quadratic-form methods or direct simulation can instead calculate the approximate loss distribution.

Short option example

A long call's value is convex in spot; a short call loses that increasing value when spot rises. Gamma amplifies short-call loss under a large upward move. Delta alone extrapolates the local slope and can understate this effect. Time decay contributes separately: for a short option it may offset some losses, but it does not remove the nonlinear exposure.

The figure uses physical spot scenarios for the horizon and Black–Scholes valuation inside each scenario. Spot starts at 100, strike is 100, annual volatility is 25%, the risk-free rate is 2%, initial maturity is half a year and physical drift is 6%. Future maturity is reduced by one trading day. The short position's loss is the future call price minus the current price. Rates and implied volatility are held constant to isolate spot curvature and time.

Full revaluation

Full revaluation evaluates the pricing function at each scenario's future factors and remaining maturity. It captures the nonlinearity of that function, but only for risk factors actually simulated. Holding implied volatility fixed is still a model assumption; changing volatility surfaces, correlations, dividends or exercise behavior can matter substantially.

Large scenario moves may enter a region where a local Taylor expansion is inaccurate. Third and higher derivatives, barriers, digital payoffs and exercise discontinuities can make even delta–gamma unreliable. Compare approximations with full revaluation over the tail region, not just around the current spot where the expansion was fitted.

Simulation cost and pricing noise

A book with complex derivatives may need expensive pricing in every market scenario. Nested Monte Carlo uses outer physical scenarios and inner pricing simulations. Inner pricing noise can contaminate the outer tail ordering, changing both VaR and ES. Increasing outer paths alone does not remove that error. Variance reduction, common random numbers, surrogate models and adaptive allocation can help, provided their approximation error is validated.

Separate the scenario model from the valuation model in reports. A correctly implemented risk-neutral option pricer cannot establish that the physical market scenarios are realistic. Conversely, a realistic scenario distribution cannot repair an inaccurate instrument valuation.

15 / Simulation

Monte Carlo risk estimation

Monte Carlo draws scenarios from a specified probability model, revalues the portfolio and estimates the resulting loss quantile and tail mean. The steps are: define the forecast information set, simulate jointly distributed market changes, compute horizon values, form losses and apply a documented empirical risk estimator.

The empirical VaR and ES formulas are the same as in historical simulation when simulations have equal probability. What changes is where the scenarios come from. Historical estimation uses recorded shocks; Monte Carlo samples a model that may create unobserved combinations and more extreme values. Additional simulated paths reduce sampling noise within that model, rather than establish the model's truth.

Quantile precision

Under IID sampling, a continuous distribution and a positive regular density f(qα)f(q_\alpha), the sample quantile has the first-order standard error:

SE(q^α)≈α(1−α)Nf(qα).\operatorname{SE}(\widehat q_\alpha)\approx \frac{\sqrt{\alpha(1-\alpha)}}{\sqrt N\,f(q_\alpha)}.
(27)

Low density around the quantile means that a small probability error translates into a large loss error. This explains why extreme quantiles are difficult to estimate. For standard normal loss at 99%, the standard error multiplier is about 3.73/N3.73/\sqrt N; its size comes from the thin density at the boundary.

Expected Shortfall precision

For a smooth distribution and sufficiently many moments, the ES influence function can be written as:

IFES(ℓ)=(ℓ−qα)+1−α−(ESα−qα).\operatorname{IF}_{\mathrm{ES}}(\ell) =\frac{(\ell-q_\alpha)_+}{1-\alpha} -(\operatorname{ES}_\alpha-q_\alpha).
(28)

Its variance divided by NN gives the first-order sampling variance of the plug-in ES estimator. The first-order derivative associated with estimating the boundary cancels in this representation. Simply calculating the ordinary standard error of observed tail losses and ignoring the random boundary is not a general derivation of ES uncertainty.

Finite ES does not guarantee a finite asymptotic ES variance. A heavy-tailed model can have a finite first moment and infinite second moment, so the usual square-root-NN normal approximation may fail. The laboratory uses finite-variance Student-t models with ν>2\nu>2; small samples can still depart materially from asymptotic approximations.

Tail counts and reproducibility

The expected tail count is N(1−α)N(1-\alpha). At 99.9%, even 10,000 scenarios represent only ten observations' worth of empirical tail mass. More scenarios or specialized rare-event methods may be needed. Reporting many decimal places does not compensate for a small tail sample.

Save the random seed, generator, model parameters and valuation version. Repeating a fixed seed helps compare code changes; changing seeds helps reveal simulation variability. Importance sampling and weighted scenarios can improve rare-event efficiency, but then the estimator must use the likelihood weights correctly and its uncertainty calculation must match the sampling design.

For uncertainty attributable only to simulation, compare with an analytical benchmark whenever one exists. For uncertainty in fitted parameters, refit or perturb the model. For model uncertainty, compare justified alternative distributions and stress scenarios. These are separate questions and require separate experiments.

16 / Conditional models

Volatility filtering and conditional risk

Financial volatility often changes over time. A return that was routine in a volatile period can be unusually large in a quiet one. Filtered historical simulation estimates historical conditional means and volatilities, standardizes past observations, then rescales the residual scenarios to today's forecast conditions.

Rt=μt+σtεt,ε^t=Rt−μ^tσ^t,Rt+1(i)=μ^t+1+σ^t+1ε^i.R_t=\mu_t+\sigma_t\varepsilon_t,\qquad \widehat\varepsilon_t=\frac{R_t-\widehat\mu_t}{\widehat\sigma_t},\qquad R_{t+1}^{(i)}=\widehat\mu_{t+1}+\widehat\sigma_{t+1}\widehat\varepsilon_i.
(29)

The analogy is comparing storms after accounting for local weather conditions: a 3% move on a normally quiet day carries different information from the same move during a high-volatility episode. Standardization tries to make shocks comparable before applying them to the current forecast scale.

EWMA and GARCH

An exponentially weighted moving-average variance forecast uses earlier residuals. With σt2\sigma_t^2 known before observing date-tt residual at=Rt−μta_t=R_t-\mu_t, the next forecast is:

σt+12=λσt2+(1−λ)at2.\sigma_{t+1}^2=\lambda\sigma_t^2+(1-\lambda)a_t^2.
(30)

A GARCH(1,1) model adds an intercept and separates shock and persistence parameters:

σt+12=ω+aat2+bσt2,ω>0,a,b≥0.\sigma_{t+1}^2=\omega+a\,a_t^2+b\,\sigma_t^2,\quad \omega>0,\ a,b\ge0.
(31)

Under the usual normalized innovation assumptions, a+b<1a+b<1 gives a finite stationary unconditional variance ω/(1−a−b)\omega/(1-a-b). EWMA corresponds to a zero-intercept, unit-persistence variance recursion and lacks that same finite long-run mean-reversion structure. Parameter conditions and the innovation distribution jointly determine which higher moments exist.

Correct forecast timing

Use σt\sigma_t, estimated from information available before date tt, to standardize the date-tt observation. Updating volatility with ata_t and then using the updated value as the forecast that supposedly existed before ata_t is observed leaks future information. The figure explicitly plots pre-observation risk forecasts; the response to a shock occurs in subsequent forecasts.

A filtered scenario model assumes that standardized innovations are sufficiently stable. Check residual autocorrelation, remaining squared-residual dependence, tail behavior and regime changes. Filtering can remove conditional variance dynamics without eliminating jumps or a changing tail shape. A fitted normal GARCH model and a historical residual bootstrap are different innovation models.

Multivariate and multi-day extensions

For multiple factors, preserve residual dependence across same-date observations or specify a joint standardized-shock model. Individually filtered residuals should not automatically be shuffled independently. Changing correlations can require a dynamic covariance model or explicit stressed dependence assumptions.

For multi-day forecasts, update simulated volatility recursively along each simulated path. Reusing today's scale at every future day is a frozen-volatility approximation. Filtered historical simulation and conditional extreme-value models share this idea of separating dynamic scale from residual tail shape; McNeil and Frey (2000) study the latter combination.

17 / Tail models

Extreme-value theory and tail extrapolation

Extreme-value theory concentrates modeling effort on observations above a high threshold. The peaks-over-threshold approach approximates the conditional excess Y=L−uY=L-u, given L>uL>u, by a generalized Pareto distribution. Its survival function is:

ℙ(Y>y|L>u)≈(1+ξyβ)−1/ξ,β>0,y≥0,1+ξy/β>0.\mathbb P(Y>y\mid L>u)\approx \left(1+\xi\frac{y}{\beta}\right)^{-1/\xi}, \quad \beta>0,\ y\ge0,\ 1+\xi y/\beta>0.
(32)

For ξ=0\xi=0, the limiting survival function is e−y/βe^{-y/\beta}. Positive shape ξ\xi gives a heavy, unbounded tail. Negative shape gives a finite upper endpoint. The approximation is motivated by asymptotic tail theory; it is not a claim that every finite threshold produces an exact generalized Pareto law.

VaR and ES beyond the threshold

Let pu=ℙ(L>u)p_u=\mathbb P(L>u), estimated by the threshold exceedance fraction in a basic IID model. For a target tail probability p=1−α<pup=1-\alpha<p_u, solving the survival equation gives:

qα≈u+βξ[(pu1−α)ξ−1],ξ≠0.q_\alpha\approx u+\frac{\beta}{\xi} \left[\left(\frac{p_u}{1-\alpha}\right)^\xi-1\right],\qquad \xi\ne0.
(33)
qα≈u+βln(pu1−α)(ξ=0),ESα≈qα+β+ξ(qα−u)1−ξ(ξ<1).q_\alpha\approx u+\beta\ln\!\left(\frac{p_u}{1-\alpha}\right)\quad(\xi=0),\qquad \operatorname{ES}_\alpha\approx q_\alpha+ \frac{\beta+\xi(q_\alpha-u)}{1-\xi}\quad(\xi<1).
(34)

The scale of excesses above the new quantile is β+ξ(qα−u)\beta+\xi(q_\alpha-u). Dividing it by 1−ξ1-\xi gives their conditional mean, provided ξ<1\xi<1. ES becomes extremely sensitive as shape approaches one. For ξ≥1\xi\ge1, this model's upper-tail mean is infinite; a finite numerical answer would conceal a failure of the moment condition.

The threshold trade-off

A low threshold supplies many observations but can include data outside the asymptotic tail regime. A high threshold improves the plausibility of the approximation while leaving few excesses and unstable parameter estimates. Inspect threshold stability, mean-excess plots, quantile diagnostics and uncertainty bands. A single fitted shape estimate without sensitivity analysis is weak evidence for a precise extreme ES.

For an exact generalized Pareto tail, raising the threshold preserves shape and changes scale linearly. This motivates stability diagnostics, but samples can be too short to reveal a stable region clearly. An extrapolated 99.99% quantile from a small dataset is driven heavily by the chosen tail family and shape.

Dependence and conditioning

Serially clustered extremes violate a basic IID fitting interpretation. Volatility filtering, declustering or a dependence-aware analysis can help, each with its own assumptions. Modeling standardized conditional residuals is different from fitting a Pareto tail directly to unconditional returns. For weighted history, replacing counts with weights is not automatically a valid likelihood derivation.

EVT extends a model beyond the largest observed loss, which is useful and also makes extrapolation risk explicit. Unlike a stress test, it assigns probabilities through a statistical tail model. Unlike plain historical simulation, it can generate previously unseen magnitudes. Document which part of the distribution is empirical and which part is extrapolated.

18 / Model risk

Tail dependence, stress and liquidity

Correlation measures linear co-movement across the distribution. Tail dependence asks whether one variable's extreme outcome makes another variable's extreme outcome persistently more likely as the threshold moves outward. For continuous loss marginals, upper-tail dependence is:

λU=limu↑1ℙ(L2>qu(L2)|L1>qu(L1)),\lambda_U=\lim_{u\uparrow1} \mathbb P(L_2>q_u(L_2)\mid L_1>q_u(L_1)),
(35)

provided the limit exists. A nonsingular Gaussian copula has zero asymptotic tail dependence, despite positive dependence at ordinary thresholds. A Student-t copula can have positive tail dependence even when its correlation parameter matches the Gaussian copula's. The shared random scale creates scenarios in which several factors become extreme together.

The figure plots the population upper-tail dependence coefficient for two t-copula degrees of freedom. Zero asymptotic Gaussian tail dependence should not be described as zero probability of joint losses, nor does it imply that a Gaussian model is always an inappropriate approximation. It identifies a specific difference in the extreme limit.

Stress scenarios complement probabilistic tails

A stress scenario asks what the book loses under a specified adverse configuration. It can combine an equity drop, a volatility increase, curve changes, widening spreads and a liquidity shock. Unless calibrated through a probability model, it does not have an implied confidence level. A €200,000 stress loss should not be called a 99.9% VaR merely because it is large.

Historical crises supply interpretable scenario templates. Hypothetical scenarios can address exposures absent from historical episodes. Reverse stress testing starts with a loss or business-failure threshold and asks which plausible factor combinations would cross it. Report the factor changes and valuation assumptions so that the result is reproducible.

Liquidity and endogenous effects

Mark-to-market losses assume a valuation at a modeled horizon, but selling a large position can incur bid–ask costs, price impact and delayed execution. A liquidation loss can add a cost function that depends on quantity, market depth and the liquidation schedule. If price impact is nonlinear in position size, positive homogeneity of the total loss-based risk may no longer hold.

Margin calls and funding constraints can force trades at adverse times. Correlations and liquidity can deteriorate together in a stress episode. These feedback mechanisms are not captured simply by adding a fixed percentage to a normal VaR. A model should state whether it measures valuation risk, liquidation risk or a strategy under funding constraints.

A practical report can combine a central forecast, several alternative tail models and a set of stress losses. Disagreements are informative: they reveal which exposure or assumption determines the tail. Averaging incompatible risk numbers without interpreting their underlying experiments can obscure that information.

19 / Risk attribution

Marginal and component risk

A portfolio risk number is more actionable when its source is identified. Let losses depend on exposure vector ww, and let ρ(w)\rho(w) be a differentiable, positively homogeneous risk measure. Euler's theorem yields:

ρ(w)=∑i=1dwi∂ρ(w)∂wi,RCi=wi∂ρ(w)∂wi.\rho(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}w_i\frac{\partial\rho(w)}{\partial w_i}, \qquad \operatorname{RC}_i=w_i\frac{\partial\rho(w)}{\partial w_i}.
(36)

The derivative is marginal risk: the local change per unit of added exposure. Component risk multiplies that derivative by the current exposure. Component contributions sum to total risk under the stated assumptions. They can be negative for hedging positions; a negative contribution does not mean the position has no standalone risk.

Normal portfolio formulas

For return weights with wealth WW, portfolio standard deviation σp=wTΣw>0\sigma_p=\sqrt{w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w}>0, and normal ES multiplier kα=φ(zα)/(1−α)k_\alpha=\phi(z_\alpha)/(1-\alpha), the marginal ES is:

∂ESα∂wi=−Wμi+Wkα(Σw)iσp.\frac{\partial\operatorname{ES}_\alpha}{\partial w_i} =-W\mu_i+W k_\alpha\frac{(\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma_p}.
(37)

The corresponding VaR expression replaces kαk_\alpha with zαz_\alpha. These derivatives treat weights as exposure coordinates before imposing a budget constraint. A budget-preserving trade that buys asset ii and sells asset jj has directional risk derivative equal to the difference of their marginal risks.

Tail-conditional contributions

If scenario loss is a linear combination L(w)=∑iwiℓiL(w)=\sum_i w_i\ell_i, the distribution is sufficiently regular and there is no quantile atom, marginal ES can be expressed as:

∂ESα∂wi=𝔼[ℓi|L(w)>qα].\frac{\partial\operatorname{ES}_\alpha}{\partial w_i} =\mathbb E[\ell_i\mid L(w)>q_\alpha].
(38)

The position's importance is determined by what it does in portfolio-tail scenarios, rather than its average behavior across all scenarios. In an empirical distribution, use the same fractional boundary mass as the portfolio ES estimator. When tied losses create nondifferentiability, subgradients and allocation rules may not be unique. Arbitrarily breaking ties can change attribution while leaving total ES unchanged.

Incremental risk

Incremental risk is the finite difference between risk with and without a trade. It differs from a derivative when the trade is large or reshapes the tail. Removing a position can change which scenarios enter ES, so its incremental risk need not equal its Euler component. Report which attribution convention is being used.

For a nonlinear portfolio, losses may not be homogeneous in exposure because of impact, nonlinear financing or strategy rules. Check the assumptions before enforcing a sum-to-total decomposition. Numerical finite differences should reuse scenarios to reduce simulation noise and should be checked across several perturbation sizes.

20 / Portfolio choice

Expected Shortfall portfolio optimization

Expected Shortfall can be represented as the minimum of an auxiliary threshold objective. For integrable losses:

ESα(L)=minθ∈ℝ{θ+11−α𝔼[(L−θ)+]}.\operatorname{ES}_\alpha(L)=\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R} \left\{\theta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(L-\theta)_+]\right\}.
(39)

A minimizing threshold is an α\alpha-quantile; with flat regions or atoms, the set of minimizers may contain multiple values. The minimum is ES regardless of that possible nonuniqueness. Away from atoms the derivative of the objective is 1−ℙ(L>θ)/(1−α)1-\mathbb P(L>\theta)/(1-\alpha), so the optimum balances the probability above the threshold with the specified tail mass.

This representation, developed by Rockafellar and Uryasev (2000), is especially useful when scenario losses are affine in portfolio positions. Each excess-loss term is convex, so the scenario objective is convex in the threshold and the positions.

A linear-program formulation

For scenario probabilities pjp_j, introduce auxiliary excess variables zjz_j. Minimize the following objective subject to the excess constraints and the desired investment constraints:

minw,θ,zθ+11−α∑j=1Npjzj,zj≥Lj(w)−θ,zj≥0.\min_{w,\theta,z}\ \theta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^{N}p_jz_j, \qquad z_j\ge L_j(w)-\theta,\quad z_j\ge0.
(40)

If each Lj(w)L_j(w) is affine and the feasible portfolio set is described by linear constraints, this is a linear program. Typical constraints include full investment, no short selling, bounds on individual positions and a minimum estimated return. Transaction costs can be incorporated if their chosen formulation preserves convexity.

Optimization does not remove estimation risk

An optimizer can exploit peculiarities of the sample: a position may appear attractive because the scenarios contain few events that expose its weakness. Highly confident tail objectives emphasize a small portion of the scenario set. Add position limits, turnover control, robust scenarios or other justified regularization, then evaluate the resulting portfolio outside the sample used for selection.

Compare optimized ES with the losses of practical benchmark portfolios. Sensitivity to removing one extreme date can reveal concentration in estimation information. Refit across rolling windows or bootstrap samples to inspect weight stability, while recognizing that ordinary bootstrap resampling cannot create an absent stress regime.

Convexity relies on the loss map and the constraints. Nonlinear instrument revaluation in risk factors can still be affine in quantities for a static book, which preserves scenario convexity in quantities. Position-dependent price impact, integer contracts or path-dependent trading decisions can change that structure. Define the decision variables carefully before assuming that an off-the-shelf linear solver applies.

21 / Validation

Forecast validation and regulatory context

A backtest compares forecasts that could have been made in real time with subsequently realized outcomes. At date tt, estimate the model using information available then, forecast the next horizon's risk, save that forecast and only later compare it with the realized loss. A historical fit using the entire future sample is an in-sample diagnostic, rather than a valid real-time backtest.

Rolling windows discard older observations; expanding windows retain them. Both choices should be fixed before inspecting results. If model parameters, confidence levels or trading rules are repeatedly selected on the same evaluation sample, apparent performance can reflect selection bias. Preserve a separate evaluation period or use an appropriate nested procedure.

Actual, hypothetical and modeled P&L

Actual P&L reflects the trades and events that occurred. Hypothetical P&L typically holds a specified prior portfolio fixed to isolate market changes. Risk-theoretical P&L uses the risk model's factors and valuation conventions. These series need not agree. A breach can indicate a distributional miss, an omitted factor, a valuation mismatch or a position convention mismatch.

Choose the P&L series consistently with the forecast experiment. Reconcile cash flows, fees, intraday trades and valuation timestamps. A risk forecast can have correct exception frequency against one P&L definition and poor alignment with another because the underlying books differ. Investigating exceptions often reveals more than reporting a test statistic alone.

What the Basel framework specifies

The Basel market-risk internal models framework specifies a one-tailed 97.5% ES confidence level and a ten-day base liquidity horizon, with prescribed liquidity-horizon adjustments, stressed calibration and additional requirements. VaR-based backtesting and P&L attribution remain distinct model-validation elements. The relevant official source is the BIS Basel Framework, MAR32–MAR33.

This educational laboratory calculates generic distributional risk. It does not reproduce the full regulatory capital calculation, liquidity-horizon aggregation, default-risk charge or non-modellable risk-factor treatment. Confidence and horizon parameters alone are insufficient to turn a generic ES estimate into a regulatory capital figure. Consult the applicable framework and jurisdictional rules for such a calculation.

Validation layers

Use several layers of evidence: reconcile inputs and valuation, check distributional diagnostics, evaluate exceptions and tail severity, assess performance by regime and inspect sensitivity to modeling choices. Statistical failure is evidence against a specific null hypothesis; statistical non-rejection is not proof that all relevant risks are modeled correctly.

Forecast accuracy and business usefulness also differ. A statistically calibrated risk model can respond too slowly to an emerging exposure or omit a scenario needed for a decision. Risk limits, stress tests and liquidity analysis complement the probability forecast.

22 / Backtesting

Unconditional coverage and the Kupiec test

For continuous conditional loss distributions, define a VaR breach indicator using the risk forecast qtq_t that existed before loss LtL_t was observed. At confidence α\alpha, the target breach probability is p=1−αp=1-\alpha.

It=𝟙{Lt>qt},K=∑t=1TIt.I_t=\mathbb 1_{\{L_t>q_t\}},\qquad K=\sum_{t=1}^{T}I_t.
(41)

Under correct conditional quantiles and the standard IID hit null, KK is binomial with parameters TT and pp. The observed breach rate is p^=K/T\widehat p=K/T. The unconditional coverage likelihood ratio compares the target probability with the fitted breach rate:

LRuc=−2ln[(1−p)T−KpK(1−p^)T−Kp^K].\operatorname{LR}_{\mathrm{uc}} =-2\ln\!\left[ \frac{(1-p)^{T-K}p^K} {(1-\widehat p)^{T-K}\widehat p^K} \right].
(42)

In a regular large-sample setting the statistic is asymptotically chi-squared with one degree of freedom. The test checks whether the overall breach rate is compatible with the target. It does not check when breaches occur or how severe their losses are. Kupiec (1995) emphasizes the difficulty of verifying very small tail probabilities with finite observations.

Boundary cases and finite samples

Compute likelihoods in logs to avoid underflow. Use the limiting convention 0ln0=00\ln0=0, so zero breaches or all breaches still have well-defined maximized log likelihoods. A formula that evaluates 0×ln00\times\ln0 naively may return a non-number despite a finite theoretical result.

With 250 days and 99% confidence, the expected count is 2.5. Under an IID calibrated model, the probability of zero breaches is 0.992500.99^{250}, approximately 8.1%. A quiet year is therefore not proof of an overconservative model. Sparse counts also make the asymptotic chi-squared approximation questionable; an exact binomial calculation or simulated null distribution can be more informative.

Test choices

An exact test still requires a stated rejection rule. A two-sided test based on tail probabilities and one based on probabilities of outcomes no more likely than the observed count can differ because the binomial distribution is discrete. Document the method and avoid describing a confidence interval's exclusion rule as universally equivalent to every exact two-sided test.

For losses with atoms at the forecast quantile, the strict exceedance probability can be below 1−α1-\alpha even when the quantile is correct. The continuous-hit null then needs adjustment. A randomized probability integral transform can allocate boundary mass deliberately, but an operational breach rule may reasonably choose another convention. Mathematical calibration and operational exception definitions must be distinguished.

Overlapping horizon losses, changing forecast parameters and serially dependent hits also affect inference. Report evaluation length, confidence level, breach count, timing and the assumed null. A p-value describes evidence under that null, rather than the probability that the model is correct.

23 / Backtesting

Independence and conditional coverage

A model can get the total number of breaches right while missing volatility dynamics. If most exceptions occur in one episode, the conditional forecast may have underestimated risk during that period and overestimated it elsewhere. Testing the sequence, rather than only the count, addresses this weakness.

Count transitions nijn_{ij} from breach state ii to state jj, with i,j∈{0,1}i,j\in\{0,1\}. There are T−1T-1 adjacent transitions. The unrestricted first-order Markov breach probabilities and pooled probability are:

π^01=n01n00+n01,π^11=n11n10+n11,π^=n01+n11T−1.\widehat\pi_{01}=\frac{n_{01}}{n_{00}+n_{01}},\qquad \widehat\pi_{11}=\frac{n_{11}}{n_{10}+n_{11}},\qquad \widehat\pi=\frac{n_{01}+n_{11}}{T-1}.
(43)

Independence requires the next breach probability to be the same after a breach and after a non-breach. Compare the Markov likelihood with the independent likelihood:

LRind=−2ln(1−π^)n00+n10π^n01+n11(1−π^01)n00π^01n01(1−π^11)n10π^11n11.\operatorname{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}=-2\ln \frac{(1-\widehat\pi)^{n_{00}+n_{10}}\widehat\pi^{n_{01}+n_{11}}} {(1-\widehat\pi_{01})^{n_{00}}\widehat\pi_{01}^{n_{01}} (1-\widehat\pi_{11})^{n_{10}}\widehat\pi_{11}^{n_{11}}}.
(44)

Under regularity and adequate transition counts, this has an asymptotic chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom. Conditional coverage combines it with the unconditional coverage statistic:

LRcc=LRuc+LRind∼χ22asymptotically under the null.\operatorname{LR}_{\mathrm{cc}}= \operatorname{LR}_{\mathrm{uc}}+\operatorname{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}} \ \sim\ \chi^2_2\quad\text{asymptotically under the null}.
(45)

Christoffersen (1998) develops conditional interval-forecast evaluation. The first-order transition test checks one form of dependence; it does not establish independence at every lag or against every forecast-information variable.

Two sequences with identical coverage

The figure's 500-day sequences each contain ten breaches at a target probability of 2%. Both have unconditional coverage statistic zero. In the dispersed sequence, the estimated probability after a breach is zero because none of the few breaches are consecutive. In the clustered sequence, nine of the ten transitions out of a breach lead to another breach, producing strong evidence of first-order clustering.

Artificial hit sequences · target confidence 98% · asymptotic p-values shown as illustrations; transition counts are sparse
SequenceBreachesCoverage LRTransitions [[00,01],[10,11]]Independence LRAsymptotic p
Dispersed10 / 5000.000000[[479, 10], [10, 0]]0.4090260.522464
